claims.text: The starting catalyst is a near-equiatomic multi-principal-element automotive alloy containing Cu, Ni, Pd, Pt, and potentially other elements.
Short post-synthesis annealing in NH3 at approximately 400 °C will induce surface nitrogen doping.
Nitrogen doping produces metal–nitrogen bonds on the catalyst.
Nitrogen doping creates stabilized surface metal-nitride phases.
Incorporated nitrogen modifies the electronic environment of surface metal atoms.
Nitrogen incorporation adjusts the adsorption energies of catalytic intermediates and adsorbates.
Metal–nitrogen coordination can improve catalytic activity and stability.
Nitrogen coordination can improve resistance to degradation through a pinning effect on coordinated metal atoms.
Adjusted adsorption energies lower the activation barriers for CO and hydrocarbon oxidation.
Nitrogen doping promotes desorption of H2O and NO or otherwise reduces poisoning by these species.
Nitrogen doping increases resistance to sintering during extended catalytic operation.
Relative to the untreated catalyst, the nitrogen-doped catalyst will exhibit greater CO and hydrocarbon oxidation activity below 150 °C.
Relative to the untreated catalyst, the nitrogen-doped catalyst will suffer less activity loss in the presence of H2O and NO.
Relative to the untreated catalyst, the nitrogen-doped catalyst will retain activity and structure better during prolonged thermal cycling and aging.
The benefits will persist under transient automotive exhaust below 150 °C and aging intended to represent vehicle-lifetime or real-driving degradation.
The nitrogen-doping intervention maintains low platinum-group-metal usage.
Excessive or nonuniform nitridation may block or deactivate active sites and reduce catalytic performance.
Failure to achieve a statistically significant improvement, exemplified by at least a 10% activity increase together with reduced poisoning and enhanced durability, would falsify the hypothesis.
